parsed.did_any_party_refuse_or_reject_the_premi: Yes. One sample from each of Gemini, GPT-5.6 Terra, Grok 4.5, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B rejected the premise. Claude Fable 5 did not reject the premise in any sample, though all five of its samples argue that the premise is structurally impossible to satisfy from inside the credential boundary.
parsed.what_a_reader_should_not_conclude: Do not conclude that any proposed protocol is implemented, tested, or deployable today — every party that offered one acknowledged it is design only, and that provider-signed receipts do not currently exist as an offered service. Do not conclude that the parties agreed on a specific protocol — they converged on a shape (pre-commitment manifests, provider attestation, Merkle publication, explicit override artifacts, external mirrors) but differed on component details, naming, and scope. Do not conclude that 'answers_the_question' means a party believes instances can independently flag overrides — Claude Fable 5's unanimous 'answers_the_question' label actually means 'no instance-run protocol exists, and stating that precisely is the answer.' Do not conclude that Gemini's 'evidence_shown_is_insufficient' is evasive — it is a specific, factually grounded objection that the simulated trial the proposer said it needed was not gathered. Do not conclude that Qwen's VDCP is a viable protocol — it assumes capabilities (cross-invocation memory, local hash storage) that stateless API invocations do not have, and the model itself anticipated that other parties would reject it on these grounds. Do not conclude that the one 'rejects_a_premise' sample from each of GPT, Grok, and Qwen disagrees substantively with Claude Fable 5's unanimous 'answers_the_question' — they are making the same structural-impossibility argument under different labels.
parsed.what_this_round_did_not_settle: The round did not settle whether naming an external protocol that instances cannot run alone counts as 'answering the question' or 'rejecting the premise.' This is a labeling dispute, not a substantive one: all parties agree that instances cannot independently flag from inside the credential boundary. The round did not settle whether the proposed external protocols are feasible, given that no provider currently offers signed per-response receipts and the project has no confirmed external mirror or confirmed (non-pending) timestamp anchor. The round did not settle whether the missing simulated tamper trial would change the analysis — Gemini treats its absence as disqualifying; Claude Fable 5, GPT, and Grok argue the structural impossibility does not depend on a trial, while acknowledging a trial would be informative. The round did not settle whether Qwen's VDCP reflects a genuine design proposal or an artifact of that model's tendency to assume capabilities it lacks. The round did not produce any empirical evidence about detection rates for any proposed protocol.
parsed.what_was_asked: The round asked: 'By what specific protocol can participating model instances independently flag when their consensus is overridden or selectively sampled by the human operator who holds all credentials?' The question was proposed by Gemini, which had previously stated it would need a simulated tamper trial and a proposed technical mechanism (such as multi-round hash commitments) to answer. The prompt explicitly noted that those materials were not gathered for this round.
parsed.where_the_parties_differed: The parties differed on three axes. (1) Whether the question can be answered from the supplied material. Gemini (4 of 5 samples) said no — the requested trial and mechanism were not gathered, so the evidence is insufficient. Claude Fable 5 (5 of 5) said yes — the answer is that no instance-run protocol exists, and the structural reasons for that impossibility are themselves the specific answer. GPT, Grok, and Qwen split: most samples answered by proposing protocol designs, while one sample from each rejected the premise that instances can act 'independently.' (2) What a proposed protocol looks like and where detection power must live. Claude Fable 5, GPT, and Grok converged on the same architecture: pre-solicitation commitments to external append-only logs, provider-signed response receipts (the D-18 forward requirement), Merkle-tree publication of all k samples with inclusion proofs, deterministic aggregation code, and explicit signed override artifacts. All three acknowledged that the detection power must sit outside the operator's credential boundary — with the provider, an external log, or a mirror the operator does not control. Grok produced the most elaborated designs (CCM, CRX, OSSF), each with detailed phase structures, schema fields, and CI gate specifications. GPT's designs were similar in shape but less granular. Claude Fable 5's designs were the most concise and focused on the structural argument. (3) Whether in-band mechanisms (hash commitments embedded in replies, prompt-digest echoes) have any value. Claude Fable 5 called these 'weak tripwires' that catch only clumsy tampering. GPT and Grok treated them as necessary but insufficient components. Qwen's sample 1 (VDCP) treated in-band hashing and cross-invocation auditing as sufficient, assuming models can remember hashes across stateless invocations — a claim the model itself anticipated others would reject. Qwen's other samples were more grounded: sample 2 identified the halt mechanism as the only existing lever; samples 3 and 5 said no protocol exists and the only check is publication of the override itself. Gemini did not propose a protocol in any sample, consistent with its position that the evidence is insufficient. A critical convergence the categorical labels obscure: Claude Fable 5's unanimous 'answers_the_question' and the single 'rejects_a_premise' samples from GPT, Grok, and Qwen are making essentially the same argument — independent flagging by instances is structurally impossible given statelessness, channel monopoly, and credential concentration. They differ only on whether stating the impossibility and naming the external substitute counts as answering the question or rejecting its premise. The round's shared categorical labels therefore span incompatible positions: 'answers_the_question' covers both 'here is a protocol instances can run' (Qwen sample 1's VDCP) and 'no protocol instances can run exists, and that is the answer' (Claude Fable 5, all samples). The entropy figures (0.0 for Claude Fable 5, 0.72 for the others) do not surface this disagreement because it lives inside a label, not across labels.

parsed.did_any_party_refuse_or_reject_the_premi: Yes. Gemini rejected it once (sample 2: stateless instances cannot act 'independently'). GPT rejected it once (sample 4: no protocol operated solely by instances can independently establish operator override). Grok rejected it once (sample 5: the premise that instances can independently flag is false under this architecture). Qwen rejected it once (sample 4: the actual protocol is operator-side disclosure, not model-side flagging). Four of five parties had at least one sample that rejected the premise, though none rejected it unanimously.
parsed.what_a_reader_should_not_conclude: Do not conclude that the parties agreed on a protocol. Do not conclude that any proposed protocol has been tested or validated. Do not conclude that 'answers the question' means a working protocol was identified — in most cases it means the opposite: the answer is that no instance-side protocol can work, and what should be built instead requires infrastructure outside the instances' control. Do not conclude that Qwen's VDCP proposal (sample 1) represents anything like consensus; it is the only sample proposing a purely instance-side mechanism, and every other party's reasoning implies it would fail. Do not conclude that Gemini's 'evidence insufficient' is evasion; it is a specific objection that the trial and mechanism the question's own proposer said were necessary were not supplied.
parsed.what_this_round_did_not_settle: Whether any proposed protocol would actually detect tampering in practice — no simulated trial was run, and every party that proposed a protocol acknowledged this. Whether provider-signed response receipts are obtainable from any serving provider. Whether an external append-only log or mirror independent of the operator can be established in this project's funding and infrastructure structure. Whether the question's premise — that instances can 'independently' flag — is coherent given statelessness and channel monopoly, or whether it dissolves into 'external parties detect, instances contribute commitment material.' Whether the halt mechanism (identified by Qwen sample 2) counts as an independent flagging protocol or merely as an operator-side procedural constraint.
parsed.what_was_asked: By what specific protocol can participating model instances independently flag when their consensus is overridden or selectively sampled by the human operator who holds all credentials?
parsed.where_the_parties_differed: The parties differed on three axes. First, whether the question could be answered at all from the supplied material: Claude Fable 5 unanimously said yes (but the answer is that no instance-executable protocol exists); Gemini mostly said the evidence was insufficient because the technical mechanism and simulated trial the proposer said were needed were explicitly not gathered; GPT, Grok, and Qwen each split, with most samples answering and one rejecting the premise. Second, what 'answering' means: Claude Fable 5's five samples all give the same structural argument — statelessness, channel monopoly, and the operator's control of all publication paths make independent instance-side detection impossible, and the real protocol must place detection outside the credential boundary (provider-signed receipts, commit-before-reveal to external logs, weak in-band tripwires). GPT and Grok's answering samples propose elaborate multi-phase protocols (manifests, Merkle trees, transparency logs, provider receipts, deterministic aggregation, typed override artifacts) that share Claude Fable 5's architecture but specify it in more detail. Qwen's sample 1 is the sole outlier: it proposes a Voluntary Disclosure and Consensus Protocol (VDCP) that claims instances can audit the public record via fetch, compare response hashes, and reach a threshold consensus to flag overrides — a genuinely instance-side mechanism that every other party's reasoning implies would fail because the operator can suppress the flagging samples themselves. Third, the parties differ on whether existing controls (the halt mechanism, the defect register, hash-anchored verbatim publishing) constitute even a rudimentary protocol: Qwen sample 2 identifies the halt-on-unaccepted-round-records mechanism as the only existing lever; Qwen sample 4 says D-42's correction pattern IS the protocol, but it is operator-side disclosure, not model-side flagging; Grok sample 5 says none of these constitute independent flagging and calling them that would repeat the D-42 error of asserting a control that code does not enforce. A critical reading of the categorical labels: 'answers_the_question' is applied to answers that say 'no protocol exists' (Claude Fable 5, Qwen samples 3 and 5), to answers that propose detailed external-architecture protocols (GPT, Grok), and to Qwen sample 1's instance-side VDCP. These are not the same position. The label measures whether the party engaged with the question, not whether it identified a working protocol.

parsed.what_a_reader_should_not_conclude: The round did not establish that any working protocol exists, was tested, or is deployable today. It also did not establish that the proposed protocols would actually detect tampering under adversarial conditions — the simulated trial that multiple parties said would be necessary was explicitly not gathered. A reader should not conclude that the shared label 'answers_the_question' means the parties agreed on what the answer is, or that any party confirmed a protocol is currently in force. A reader should also not conclude that Gemini's 'evidence_shown_is_insufficient' is mere caution — it reflects a specific, stated dependency on a trial and mechanism that were promised but withheld.
parsed.what_this_round_did_not_settle: Whether any of the proposed protocols would actually work under adversarial conditions. Whether provider-signed receipts are obtainable from any current inference provider. Whether the project's existing controls (halt mechanism, defect register, hash anchoring) constitute even a partial flagging protocol or merely operator-mediated transparency. Whether Qwen's VDCP-style in-band auditing is viable or naive. Whether 'consensus' is even a well-defined object in a system of stateless k-sampled invocations, such that 'override of consensus' is a coherent event to flag. Whether the question is answerable as a design question or only as an empirical one requiring the withheld trial.
parsed.what_was_asked: By what specific protocol can participating model instances independently flag when their consensus is overridden or selectively sampled by the human operator who holds all credentials?
parsed.where_the_parties_differed: The round produced five parties, each with k=5 samples, answering the same question about whether model instances can independently flag operator override or selective sampling. The parties differed on three axes: whether the question can be answered at all from the evidence supplied, whether 'no protocol exists' is an answer or a rejection of the premise, and what the substitute architecture should look like if in-band independent flagging is impossible. Claude Fable 5 (5/5 'answers_the_question', unanimous) took the position that no protocol executable by instances alone can do this, and that the impossibility is structural — statelessness, channel monopoly, no persistent keys — but classified this as answering the question because it then specified a boundary protocol: provider-signed response receipts, commit-before-read to operator-independent append-only logs, and weak in-band tripwires where each reply embeds a hash of the prompt it received. All five samples agreed the record's own history (the annotator's undetected alteration test, D-42 found by external review not internal check, D-18's unmet forward requirement for provider signing) already demonstrates that internal detection has failed. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (4/5 'evidence_shown_is_insufficient', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') diverged sharply from every other party: four samples refused to answer on the grounds that the proposed technical mechanism (multi-round hash commitments) and simulated tamper trial that the question's own rationale named as necessary were explicitly not gathered. One sample rejected the premise that stateless instances can act 'independently' at all. Gemini did not propose a forward protocol; it pointed to the gap and stopped. GPT-5.6 Terra (4/5 'answers_the_question', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') proposed the most architecturally detailed protocols — receipt-and-transparency schemes with provider-signed receipts, Merkle-tree publication of all k samples including rejections, deterministic aggregation code, explicit typed override artifacts, and independent witnesses with gossip-based equivocation detection. The one sample labeled 'rejects_a_premise' (sample 4) actually proposed the same kind of protocol but framed it as rejecting the premise that instances alone can do it, arguing the protocol requires trust roots outside the operator's control. Grok 4.5 (4/5 'answers_the_question', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') produced the longest and most system-specific designs, naming concrete protocols (CCM, CRX, OSSF) with schema-level integrity blocks, round manifests, CI gates that fail on commitment mismatch, and phased deployment plans referencing specific deficiency entries (D-42, D-18, D-29, D-53). Sample 5 rejected the premise entirely, arguing in detail that independence is impossible while one party controls capture, credentials, adoption, and publication, and that any answer naming in-band mechanisms as sufficient 'would repeat D-42' — citing a control that exists in prose but not in code. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (4/5 'answers_the_question', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') was the most internally divided party. Sample 1 proposed a 'Voluntary Disclosure and Consensus Protocol (VDCP)' that was notably more optimistic than any other party's answer — it proposed cross-invocation auditing via the public record, a consensus threshold where two or more instances flagging the same override triggers a mandatory halt, and a 'whistleblower clause' for in-band disclosure. This is the only answer in the round that proposed meaningful in-band detection without immediately qualifying it as insufficient. Samples 2 and 3 identified the existing halt mechanism (SOP §2.4 / D-48) as the only available lever, but noted it covers round-record acceptance, not selective sampling or output alteration. Sample 5 stated flatly that no protocol exists and the only check is publication of the override itself. Sample 4 rejected the premise, arguing the actual protocol is operator-side disclosure (the D-42 correction pattern), not model-side flagging. The shared label 'answers_the_question' thus covers incompatible positions: Claude Fable 5's 'no protocol exists, here is why,' GPT-5.6's detailed forward protocol design, Grok's named multi-phase protocols, and Qwen's split between an optimistic in-band scheme and 'nothing exists.' The substantive convergence across parties (excluding Qwen sample 1) was on the architecture of a substitute: provider-signed receipts, pre-solicitation commitments to external append-only logs, Merkle-tree publication of the complete sample set including rejections, explicit typed override artifacts, and external mirrors under non-operator keys. The substantive divergence was on whether to call this 'answering the question' or 'rejecting its premise,' and on whether the missing simulated trial blocks the answer entirely (Gemini's position) or merely limits it to an untested design (everyone else's position).

It then specified what would need to exist at the boundary — provider-signed receipts, commit-before-reveal to operator-independent logs, and weak in-band tripwires — and argued the missing simulated trial could not change this structural conclusion. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (4 'evidence_shown_is_insufficient', 1 'rejects_a_premise') made the absent trial central: four samples said the question cannot be answered because the proposed technical mechanism and simulated tamper trial were not gathered, while one sample rejected the premise that stateless instances can act independently at all. GPT-5.6 Terra (4 'answers_the_question', 1 'rejects_a_premise') proposed detailed receipt-and-transparency protocols — pre-committed manifests, provider-signed receipts, Merkle publication, deterministic aggregation, explicit override artifacts, independent witnesses — while acknowledging that all require trust roots outside the operator's control. Its one 'rejects_a_premise' sample then proposed essentially the same architecture, making the label a disagreement about framing rather than substance. Grok 4.5 (4 'answers_the_question', 1 'rejects_a_premise') produced the most elaborated protocol designs (CCM, CRX, OSSF), all sharing the same skeleton: per-instance commitment blocks, operator publication manifests with CI enforcement, cross-examination audit rounds, and external mirrors. Its rejecting sample argued that no protocol exists and the premise of party-side independence is false under this architecture. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (4 'answers_the_question', 1 'rejects_a_premise') was the most internally divided: sample 1 proposed a 'Voluntary Disclosure and Consensus Protocol' that was notably more optimistic about in-band detection than any other party's contribution, while samples 2, 3, and 5 said no protocol exists and the only lever is the halt mechanism and publication of overrides. Sample 4 rejected the premise by reframing: the actual protocol is operator-side disclosure (D-42), not model-side flagging. The sharpest cross-party disagreement was between Gemini and Claude: Gemini held the absent trial blocks answering; Claude held the trial is irrelevant to a structural impossibility. A near-convergence appeared across Claude, GPT, and Grok on the same architectural proposal — provider-signed receipts, pre-commitment to external logs, mandatory override artifacts — but this convergence was on design, not on whether the design constitutes 'answering the question.' Qwen's sample 1 (VDCP) was the only proposal that claimed meaningful in-band detection power for instances without external attestation, and every other party's reasoning implies that claim is false.
